utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I wish good afternoon to everybody here, to all the accused, to the Defence counsel. Good afternoon to all the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and good afternoon to everybody else assisting us. I believe the Prosecution would like the floor. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, each of Your Honours, to counsel, to all those assisting us in and about the courtroom. Your Honours, I've asked to have a few moments to address the decisions that the Chamber issued on Thursday last week so that there can be, hopefully, no misunderstanding about that and the Prosecution can address the Chamber's concerns. As the Chamber may recall, this is the first time we had been in session since those issues -- excuse me, those decisions or rulings were issued on Thursday, the 5th of February, 2009. Unfortunately, Your Honours, I have not yet seen an English translation of those documents, so I have not been able to read the documents myself. Given the issues of language and translation that arise from time to time, even in the courtroom, I hope the Trial Chamber will hopefully understand and appreciate that there is often nuance and meaning in language that may be separate from or in addition to the words on the page. Therefore, while I've not been able to read the documents myself, with my apologies for not reading the French language, my understanding is that there is some indication in the Chamber's rulings that at least -- or at least implicitly that comments or statements had been expected from the Prosecution after my departure from the courtroom a few minutes before 7.00 p.m. on Tuesday, the 27th of January, 2009. Again, as just mentioned, I think this highlights, if I may submit, Your Honours, the complexities and sometimes difficulties of clear communication in an environment which involves not only different languages, but people coming from different cultures and different legal systems. So with that background in mind, let me begin my comments by responding to the apparent concern that the Prosecution has not previously said anything about the situation occurring on the evening of the 27th of January. At the beginning of the very next court session at 2.15 the following day on Wednesday, 28 January, the President, Judge Antonetti, summarised and commented on the events at the end of the previous session the evening before. My reaction to and interpretation of Judge Antonetti's comments was that it acknowledged that the previous evening's session had involved what I might call some rough edges on perhaps everyone's part, including my own. It was taken as a sort of a bad day, if you will, if I can use the vernacular, or at least that part of it, and the signal was for me that next day, at the beginning of the next session, was to complete the submissions that I had not been able to complete the previous evening and essentially for everyone to move on from there, without belabouring the matter further. I can tell the Chamber, that was at least my reaction on receiving the President's comments the next day, that it was an unfortunate situation on all sides, including my own, in which the Prosecution had been cut off, but everyone was moving on, and it was my understanding, perhaps wishful thinking, that the chapter was closed. So nothing more was said in that regard about that, and with the greatest of respect, I thought in doing so or not saying more about it, that I was acting in keeping with what I thought had been the President's observations. If I misread those comments or the Chamber's intention, then it was my honest mistake in thinking that the cue given, if you will, had been to move on. That explains -- that's my comment to Your Honours to explain why I had not raised the matter previously. Now, to move to the statement on the merits, if you will, the statement that perhaps some might have desired that I made previously but didn't, I start by quoting the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski case, which this Chamber has heard before: "The application of the concept of a fair trial in favor of both parties is understandable because the Prosecution acts on behalf of and in the interests of the International Community, including the interest of the victims of the offences charged [in cases before the Tribunal, the Prosecutor acts on behalf of the International Community]. This principle of equality does not affect the fundamental protections given by the general law or Statute to the accused, and the trial proceeds against the background of these fundamental protections. Seen in this way, it is difficult to see how a trial could ever be considered to be fair where the accused is favoured at the expense of the Prosecution, beyond a strict compliance with those fundamental protections." The Chamber will be well aware, I am sure, that the Prosecution from time to time, since the trial started in April 2006, has stated its concerns about some aspects of the trial and the methodology, and courtroom practice, and about the fairness towards the Prosecution and to the victims and the International Community which we represent. With the greatest respect, but to explain again what happened on the 27th, I must be direct but at the same time respectful. There have been times when the Prosecution has felt that it is sometimes viewed in the courtroom as an after-thought or second-class participant in these proceedings. As a broad illustration of the Prosecution's concerns, and I just say this -- I indicate this as a broad measure or indication of our concerns, one only need look at the Registry's most recent official time statistics distributed on the 30th of January, 2009. Since the beginning of the Defence cases in May 2008, the Defence have consumed approximately 38 percent of the time; the Prosecution, 26 percent; procedural matters, 20 percent; and the Judges' questions, 16 percent. Even throughout that time, you can see that the Judges' questions have only been a little less than the time taken by the Prosecution for questioning the Defence witnesses. More specifically, in the month of January 2009, the statistics were these: Defence, 34 percent; Judges' questions, 23 percent; procedure, 23 percent; Prosecution, 20 percent, the Prosecution taking up last place in the amount of time used in the courtroom. Again, Your Honours, I'm only looking at this as one broad illustration of the Prosecution's concerns. In January alone, the Defence had more than 40 percent more time -- more than 40 percent more time than the Prosecution. And in this regard I note Judge Prandler's comments on the 30th of January, 2009, concerning these same statistics. Judge Prandler stated: "Time used since commencement of the Defence case, as well as the monthly time monitoring for January 2009, let me ask all the recipients concerned, i.e., my fellow Judges, the parties, and the members of the team, to study carefully the clearly alarming number of hours used for certain purposes, especially in January." Thus, Your Honours, Mr. President, each of Your Honours, what happened on Tuesday, the 27th of January, was in the context of the Prosecution's continuing concerns about the fairness of these proceedings to the victims, to the International Community, and to the Prosecution. Part of the issues that candidly, and with respect, frustrate the Prosecution is the Prosecution's fair and reasonable ability to make its submissions in the courtroom. And with respect, we often feel that we are effectively cut out of the proceedings or given insufficient regard in that respect. I'm just telling you the Prosecution's assessment and its feelings, if you will, leading to some of the frustrations that we've had and our concerns that are not new but have gone on for some time. Now, let me turn, with that background in mind, Mr. President, to the specific event on the 27th of January, 2009. In the context of what I've just you taken a few moments to say, in connection with these very same concerns, the Prosecution felt on that evening that it was yet once again being cut out of the proceedings. After a Defence submission, which I did not interrupt, I had been given the floor, only to have the floor taken away from me by Defence interventions and, with great respect, the Chamber taking no steps to limit the Defence interventions in a situation where the Stojic Defence had been and was given considerable more time to address an issue, in fact, almost three times as much as the Prosecution, and indeed, and my argument in this respect is not with Mr. Khan but as a matter of statistics, indeed Mr. Khan was on his feet for a second time, stating his arguments again, when the Prosecution had not yet had even its first submission. I stated at the time, transcript at 36095: "Your Honours, it's unseemly for counsel to object to an argument that they have put in motion. They've raised the issue. I'm responding to it, and I did not interrupt Mr. Khan as much as I might have wanted to, and I would appreciate the same courtesy." Despite this statement and request, the Defence submissions continued on, with no intervention by the Chamber. In those circumstances and with the background of our longer-term and continuing concerns, it appeared to the Prosecution, frankly, that it had no role to play in these proceedings when, with respect, at that moment the Chamber was acting as if the Prosecution was not present and had no role to play in these proceedings. In that specific circumstance, I did leave the courtroom a few minutes before 7.00 p.m. on Tuesday, the 27th of January. I do say it was a moment of extreme frustration, cumulative frustration on my part with these issues. Now, I want to, before I close, and I am closing, Your Honours, and I do thank the Chamber for allowing me this time, I do want to recognise that the President, Judge Antonetti, addressed this same concern just last Thursday afternoon in our last session on 5th of February, when a similar pattern, if you will, was developing, and the President stated, in response to the point that I made, and I'm quoting Judge Antonetti now: "Indeed, you are right. When you have the floor and you are interrupted by somebody, this is not pleasant, and I do understand that a moment ago when you were on your feet, the Defence counsel raised objections, not knowing what you were about to say. I do subscribe to your point of view in this regard." So, Mr. President, I thank you for those observations, which really dovetail and underline the concerns that I have stated this afternoon on behalf of the Prosecution. In sum, Your Honours, and I speak both for the Prosecution, also for myself personally, I want to clearly indicate and reaffirm my utmost respect for the Chamber and for each of its members. I certainly take on board the Chamber's recent decision. While the Prosecution maintains its various concerns, and will continue to state those concerns when it feels it is appropriate to do so, I do regret departing the courtroom early, and I certainly hope and I do commit to you that there will not be another situation where the courtroom is left without Prosecution counsel in the courtroom. And thank you for receiving my comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Scott. Is there any other matter you'd like to raise? Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. And I will be very brief, just for the record noting that again today the accused Mr. Coric is not present in the courtroom. I had a brief few words with his counsel before the beginning of today's proceedings, and counsel informed me that indeed Mr. Coric would not be attending the proceedings today. And in view of that, and in view of the statement of Mr. Coric that was read into the record by his counsel last week, Mr. President, we believe that it's necessary for the Trial Chamber to make, if you will, a more detailed or a clear finding in respect of the status of Mr. Coric at this time. It's the Prosecution's view, based upon the statement that he made that was read into the record last week, in which he said that he was making -- this was a personal protest against the way in which the trial is being conducted, and that he was declining, at least for the time being, medication, that he was going to stay away from the trial, it's the Prosecution's submission, Mr. President, based upon jurisprudence of this Tribunal, as well as the ICTR, and I'm speaking specifically with respect to the Appeals Chamber decision here in the Stanisic case, the Appeals Chamber decision in the Nahimana case, the Trial Chamber decision in the Bagaragaza case out of ICTR, in which those Chambers held in that an accused's knowing, conscious decision not to come to a trial that he knew was taking place, where he'd been informed of the date and the place and the time of the trial, that in those circumstances such conduct is -- does constitute a waiver of the accused's right to be present at the trial. And it's our submission that that's the same circumstance that applies in respect of Mr. Coric. We hope that it is not going to be an issue that lasts longer than a day or two, but in any event we think that based upon the record, the Trial Chamber has grounds and ought to make an explicit finding that even though Mr. Coric has apparently declined to sign the form out at the Detention Unit on waiver of appearance, we think that the circumstances fully justify a finding that this is, in fact, a knowing, voluntary waiver of his right to appearance. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you may imagine, the Trial Chamber pondered over the issue at the end of the week and over the weekend, and even this morning. We have reflected over the situation, the various aspects of it. Last week, we decided that we were going to continue the testimony of the witness. We felt that the accused was represented by his Defence counsel and that on the basis of jurisprudence, the proceedings could go forward. The main issue for the Chamber at the moment is the health status of Mr. Coric. At this very moment, a decision is being filed. Mr. Stringer, the Chamber, more than anybody else, is very sensitive to the situation flowing from the absence of Mr. Coric, and the Chamber will take the necessary measures so that Mr. Coric is back with us as soon as possible. A decision is being filed as we speak. You will read it. It is a confidential document. There is no need to discuss it here. We are doing our utmost so that the person concerned can be back with us in the courtroom, and he will be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This being said, Mr. Stringer - and welcome everyone here - I can safely and firmly relate the attitude of the Chamber that is expressed in the decision that it passed, perhaps not in a very elaborate form last week, and that is that the law is exactly as you have now stated it. The Chamber also has no reasons at this moment to doubt the free will of Mr. Coric in waiving his right to be present at the trial against him, and therefore the trial must continue even in his absence, and he is not legally aggrieved by that and has no reason to complain under law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the witness brought in. I think the Prosecution has two hours and thirty minutes left. Mr. Scott, I believe you have two hours and thirty minutes left, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I thought, Your Honour, I thought it was a bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologies. I thought that at the end of the day, the Stojic Defence had used something around two and a half hours, we had used -- so meaning that we would get a -- sorry, five and a half hours. My apologies. That we would get the same amount of time, and that so far my understanding is that as of Thursday, we'd only used one hour and forty-five minutes. So I would have thought the number would have been substantially more than that, but we can certainly check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll make our own calculations. Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear me? Our apologies for keeping you waiting, but we had a few procedural issues to solve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bozic, and I trust you had a reasonably satisfactory weekend in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. That I had a good weekend was due to the courtesy of the Victims and Witness Unit, because to be in The Hague for 18 days is not easy, but it's much easier for me than all the rest of you sitting here in the courtroom, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bozic, and we do lift our hats to the continuing good efforts of the Victims and Witnesses Section and the good work that they do. Sir, the first topic that I would like to touch on this afternoon is the meetings of the HVO HZ-HB that you've indicated in your previous testimony that you did attend on a number of occasions. Just to confirm again a couple of basic facts, is it correct, sir, that at various times the HVO HZ-HB met at the Hotel Arrow and also at something called the Meteorological Institute?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What does "Euro" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hotel Arrow. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At both of those two locations, correct, Hotel Arrow and the Meteorological Institute?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, at least as to the meetings that you personally attended, can you tell -- can you confirm to the Chamber, based on my understanding, that Mr. Boban did not attend any of the meetings, again at least not the ones which you attended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that he didn't attend any of the meetings which I attended. He might have been present at some of those meetings, the ones that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, without taking too much time, would you agree with me if I told you that when we'd spoken in 2003, you'd indicated that Mr. Boban did not attend any of those meetings? Would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you. I said when I began talking to you that I was there as a suspect and had my rights and duties, and that I am -- I was a witness of justice in this courtroom, having taken the solemn declaration, and what I'm saying is -- I'm saying it as somebody who's taken the oath before the Honourable Trial Chamber, so I'd wish to stand by what I've already said in this courtroom, and especially because you're reminding me of certain details which I find very difficult to talk about, since they took part more than -- took place more than five and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree, would you not, that the work of the Defence Department, the HVO Department of Defence, was under the supervision of the HVO government, that is, the HVO HZ-HB; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean when you say that, "under the supervision of"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Defence Department was under the umbrella, if you will, and under the supervision of the HVO government; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time in this courtroom and thanks to the Trial Chamber, I wish to testify as somebody who was in certain places during a certain period of time, but at the same time, the knowledge I have as a lawyer, which I had then and which I have today, I do not wish to correct in any way, and I wish to express myself in precise terms, as befits a lawyer. The HVO HZ-HB was the temporary executive organ in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, that's not my question. Excuse me for cutting you off. You know, Mr. Bozic, that unfortunately our time is very limited, and I can tell you I'd be more than happy to discuss any of these matters at greater length if our time was not so limited. But my specific question to you, and you don't need to explain to me -- with respect, please, and understand that I'm not trying to be discourteous, but without discussing a broad range of topics, my question to you, sir, was very simple. The Defence Department was part of the HVO government, was it not? It was -- when we say "Defence Department," it was a department of the HVO government; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have actually corrected your own question after my remark. I said that I wanted to express myself as regulated by the rules. I appreciate the factor of time, but unfortunately because of that factor, I am in the courtroom for the fifth day and many hours, so I am telling the truth because I have taken the solemn declaration that I will speak the truth, and I may facilitate your questions if I elaborate a little. You have now changed your question in relation to your previous question. The Defence Department, like all departments, were bodies of the HVO HZ-HB, as the highest level of executive powers in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So please make your questions precise so as not to make me elaborate, have to elaborate. I wish to give you the whole truth, not just a part of the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you likewise agree, sir, that the Main Staff of the HVO was established -- I think you touched on this with one of the Defence counsel last week, but just to clarify and confirm, the Main Staff of the HVO was established within -- within and as part of the Department of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the HVO, pursuant to the decision on the organisation of the Defence Department, was a part of the Defence Department and was within that department, with a specific position of its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving forward, then: You had indicated last week, I believe it was last Tuesday, in fact, you were asked the question, "Have you seen any document signed by Mr. Stojic which, by its content, would represent the commanding of armed forces or the use of armed forces?" And your answer was, sir: "I've never seen a single one." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I'd like to you show me that document that you're asking me to comment on. You must bear in mind that I can't go back to all the questions and answers a week ago, so if you really wish me to present the truth about things I know, please make it possible for me to at least look at the document, because a large number of those documents were shown to me last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I wasn't showing you a document, sir. I was referring to your testimony under oath last week, when you were put the question: "Have you seen any document signed by Mr. Stojic which, by its content, would represent the commanding of armed forces or the use of armed forces?" It had nothing to do with any particular document put in front of you. Your answer under oath was: "I've never seen a single one," meaning, if I understand it correctly, sir, you've never seen a single document about Mr. Stojic commanding armed forces or the use of armed forces. That was your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That applied to the part when the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, has the possibility of transferring certain competencies, and I said that I never saw a document whereby Mr. Boban had transferred any of his competences of commanding the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, that's a similar question, but not exactly the same question. You were indeed asked that, and you did give an answer something like that, but there was a separate question, not about the delegation of Mr. Boban's power, but you were specifically asked about Mr. Stojic's military involvement. And I'll have to let the record speak for itself at this point, rather than arguing about what your testimony was last week. The Judges, of course, will know. Let me ask you to turn your attention to P 01155. It will be in the first binder, I believe, P 01155.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please assist me to find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would ask for the usher's assistance, please. Binder 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have it, sir? Usher, you may need -- if you could stay for a moment, because I'd like to -- in the interests of time, I'd like to show the witness three documents, related documents, which the Chamber and the courtroom is, I'm sure, familiar with. Sir, would you look at P 01155, which is a decision over the name of Jadranko Prlic, dated the 15th of January, 1993. I'd like you to look at that document just to see what it is, and I'd like to ask you to next look at Exhibit P 01140, which also should be in binder number 1. P 01140. Sir, this is a document dated the same day, titled "Order" on the 15th of January, 1993, by Mr. Stojic. In the introduction to the order above the word "Order" at the top of the first page, it makes reference to -- well, it says: "Pursuant to decision of the HVO HZ-HB number 01-I-32/93 of 15 January 1993, I hereby order:" And I will next ask you to please turn to Exhibit P 01139. It should be the immediate preceding exhibit, sir, P 01139.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is an order also of 15 January 1993, making a reference to a decision of the HZ-HB HVO and a reference to the order of the chief of the Defence Department, also dated 15 January 1993, an order over the name of Milivoj Petkovic. Sir, isn't it correct that those three documents, taken together, show the issuance and implementation of a government decision, if you will, flowing from top to bottom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe it in that way, for the simple reason that this is a rather specific situation, in view of the fact that in those days, there were intensified political negotiations seeking a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't ask whether it was exceptional, or specific, or anything. My only question to you is what the document showed. Did that show a document -- a decision by the president of the HVO government, an order -- an implementing order by the chief of the Defence Department, and an implementing order by the chief or the head of the HVO Main Staff, all dated the 15th of January, 1993; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you asked me whether it was the customary method of commanding from the government, through the department, to the Main Staff, and I said that this was specific. But looking at all three documents, it is correct that one follows from another; that is, it begins with the decision of the HVO of the HZ-HB, then it goes on with an order by the head of the Defence Department, ending with an order by the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And there was nothing in my previous question about -- and the records will show, nothing about whether this was customary or not. If there was a misstatement or translation, I apologise for that. And, sir, nothing particularly surprising about that, is there? That's what you would expect a civilian government, exercising control over the military, that that's the way the decision -- policy decision would work, would it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here, a witness under oath. I do not have to accept your remarks. I present my own views. To what extent Their Honours will accept them, it's up to them. I'm saying that this was a special, specific situation, and bear that in mind -- bearing that in mind, that produced the decisions as they were taken in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's go -- let's look at it, then, the other way around, sir. Just bear with me one moment. Isn't it also correct, sir, that as we established a few minutes ago, the HVO Main Staff was established within the Department of Defence, the Department of Defence was itself a creature of the HVO HZ-HB; was it not your experience that from time to time policy decisions or policy disputes, possibly between the HVO and the Main Staff, or some part of it, and the Department of Defence, or some part of it, would rise to the level of the HVO government for resolution? Instead of from the top down, this was coming from lower, moving up. That's the way it worked, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I don't know what you mean, dealing with certain misunderstandings or disputes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wasn't it the case, sir, that on a number of occasions - I'm not going to give you a particular number - but that if there was a dispute between the HVO Main Staff, for example, and the Department of Defence, or perhaps a dispute within the Department of Defence, that the various senior managers of that body perhaps did not agree, those disputes or differences would be, if you will, submitted to the HVO government, the higher body, for resolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I assume there are some facts to support this hypothetical. And if so, perhaps he could point them out, because we've been here for two and a half years, and I don't see -- I don't recall, at least, one instance where this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we're repeating last week's essential pattern of anticipating without knowing what the Prosecution's next question or document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do think that when you pose questions, you can't just make up facts and hypotheticals. They have to be based on something. Otherwise, it's called a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is there any indication, Your Honours, that I've made it up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, wait and see. Just wait for Mr. Scott to put his question. We need to know what his question is. Cutting him off immediately, when you don't even know where he's going, is a waste of time, more than anything. I don't know where he wants to go, I don't know what he wants to demonstrate. Let's wait and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may: On the other hand, Mr. Scott, I do not recall having my attention drawn to a dispute between General Staff and Department of Defence which then would have been submitted for resolution to the higher level, and if there is such an example, it would certainly be helpful if you could present it to the witness and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel, and the Chamber might expect that might be the exact next document that I would put before the witness and before the Chamber, if allowed the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But in any event -- but in any event, sir, but I'm entitled to ask a general question of the deputy minister of defence, and I'm putting to you, sir, and for the third or fourth time, I'm asking this question:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wasn't it the case, sir, that on occasions there might be disputes within the department or with the HVO Main Staff that would be raised to the level of the HVO government for resolution? Now you can answer that again as Mr. Karnavas says, yes, no, maybe, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer your question, but before I do that, I appeal to you -- I appeal to you, I ask you -- no, no, I'm asking you, because you keep --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, answer the question, please. The Prosecutor has a limited amount of time allocated to the presentation of his case. He's putting his case. Whether it's a good case or a bad case, we don't know yet. You might be surprised, but you were a judge, you've been a prosecutor, so you can be quite surprised at the way things proceed here, but here in this Tribunal we work along with -- according to this procedure. You may think what you want of it, but for right now the Prosecutor is controlling the game right now. So, Mr. Scott, please pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to turn to P 04756, P 04756 in binder number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, while you're looking at that further, because unfortunately we're moving at an extremely slow pace, sir, this is the minutes of a Department of Defence meeting on the 2nd of September, 1993, which everyone in the courtroom, I believe, has seen probably several times. And I would like to focus now very specifically on one part of it. If you can find item number 4, there's headings in the document named item 1, item 2, item 3, et cetera. Item 4 is on page 6 of the English version, and it talks about the status of students in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the mobilisation, if you will, of those students. After the subheadings A and B, there is this statement indicated by General Matic from the Main Staff: "I believe that all students should be engaged in military units. If a country is at war, its secondary schools and universities cease to function." Then it says: "Bagaric, Lucic, and Bozic believes that regular students should be left to pursue their studies. This, they claim, is in the Croats' best interests (because of the shortage of qualified personnel). Head Stojic believes that in this particular case, the opinion of the Main Staff of the HVO should prevail. He says that his own proposal at the next session of the government will be to engage all students in the HVO military units (those who have not done their military service yet should be sent to the regular military service)." Now, the "Bozic" that's referenced in that passage, sir, that was you, correct, Slobodan Bozic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when Mr. Bagaric and Lucic is mentioned, and the third name is Bozic, that is indeed me, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Stojic says, Well, this will be raised the at the next session of the HVO government," and I would like you then next to turn to P 05769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I did not want to intervene, but Mr. Coric is absent. If he was in the courtroom, he might have reacted. In item number 3, there something that seems to be quite important where you're playing a role, Witness. Mr. Coric is dealing with military prisons. He says there are two military prisons, the Heliodrom and Ljubuski, but he also adds that there are two other prisons, Gabela and Dretelj, which he considers not to be military prisons, and he does not personally want to be held responsible for anything regarding Dretelj and Gabela. So during that -- at that meeting, Mr. Coric took the floor and seems to be dotting the I's, dotting the Ts [as interpreted] and so forth, and then Mr. Lucic also takes the floor, saying quite the same thing as Mr. Coric, and you also take the floor. And it seems -- and you seem to say that as far as those cases are concerned, reports are required from the SIS, the military police, and the health division. It seems that Mr. Coric, Mr. Lucic, and your own words lead to the following conclusion: That there was a report required on these two prisons. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Antonetti, I remember -- I think I provided quite a precise answer to this question on the first or second day of my testimony, in answer to a question by Madam Nozica, when we spoke about this board meeting and this item that now you have quoted from, and the conclusion or, rather, the decision that reports regarding the conditions in those prisons were made by the SIS and Mr. Lucic, and that they were, as such, directly forwarded to Mr. Boban. I don't remember whether that was on the first or the second day of my testimony, but I think that I have provided a precise answer to that question, and I agree with your comments that you have just made regarding this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was on my feet before Madam Nozica. I think there was probably a mistake when you read the document, because in item 3, when you said that something was said by Mr. Coric, it was said by the head of the department. The sentence when he says that there were only two military prisons, that part was a statement by the head and not by Mr. Coric. Also, another part of the text that you read out was a quote from Mr. Lucic. So I just wanted to draw your attention to this, that there was probably a mistake in the quote, so it must be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There might have been an error in the English translation, in the English interpretation of the text I read. What I see in the text is the following: Mr. Coric raises the problem and Mr. Lucic answers. Then Mr. Bozic takes the floor. In a nutshell, Witness, I would like to know whether this issue of prisons divided was something that the members who were at the meeting did not agree on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. On the contrary, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I think that we all shared the same view and we wanted things to be resolved, because there were -- there was information indicating that the situation in Dretelj and Gabela, which, in fact, did not belong to the Defence Department, we agreed that the Defence Department had only two prisons, and that is Heliodrom and Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we should let Mr. Scott continue, because this was -- we have dealt with this last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, before Judge Trechsel took the floor, I wanted to say the following: If the sentence in quotes is not said by Mr. Coric, then it must have been said by Mr. Stojic. So you talked about the military prisons, about Gabela and Dretelj; you're the one who uttered this sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were all in agreement, all of those present at that meeting, that the prisons Heliodrom and Ljubuski belonged to the Defence Department, and not Gabela and Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, this does take us off topic, but since we've gone this far, let me try to clarify the record just a bit. Sir, you said everybody at the meeting was in agreement, but in fact -- in fact, just the opposite. Mr. Lucic was quite pointedly rejecting the position stated by Mr. Stojic. Mr. Lucic, in that section, says -- and let me back up for a moment. There is a reference to Mr. Coric earlier in the page under item 3, but when it refers to the head, about halfway down page 4, Your Honours, in the English: "Following Coric's contribution, head Stojic made the following proposals:" And then we got down to the sentence where it says: "Military prisons are another example of very bad work. The head took the floor and said ..." I put it to you, Mr. Bozic, that's Mr. Stojic talking, and contrary to what you're telling this Chamber, that there was agreement, Mr. Lucic comes in and says in so many words, "Not so fast, Mr. Stojic. You can't simply brush off the problems of Gabela and Dretelj quite so easily." Now, wasn't that the nature of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do have to intervene. Mr. Scott is angered by our interventions, but his interpretations are really impermissible. Let us read out what it says here. Let us read the document. The document is in front of us, and it clearly says what Mr. Lucic says. And I wish to remind you, as His Honour Judge Trechsel has recalled, I did read out passages from this document, and we read out what Mr. Lucic said, but it certainly isn't what my learned friend has just said. So let's read out what Mr. Lucic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic says, sir, at the top of page 5 in the English version: "I believe that we cannot just pass over the problem of the Gabela and Dretelj prisons like that." I think I read that correctly. That was the conversation at the meeting in that regard, was it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, your previous interpretation, as well as this one, gives me the impression that we're not reading the same text, because your interpretation does not correspond to the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, but time is precious. I'm not interpreting anything. I read directly. Everyone -- the Judges have seen, I quoted the document verbatim. It has nothing to do with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Permit me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back to the questions that I wanted to put to you, and I'm sure if the Chamber wants to come back on this topic, I'm sure the Chamber will do so, and I would not blame it if it did. But let me go back to the topic for which I took you to this document. Sir, if you will look again at item 4, we talked about that, and now that some minutes has passed, I'm forced to go back and refresh the courtroom's memory about the issue of the mobilisation of students, and we talked about that. You identified yourself as one of the participants in that conversation. I had next asked you to go to P 05769. You have that, sir? P 05759 [sic], in the first binder. You will recall, sir, that what Mr. Stojic said in the previous document, that he would raise this issue at the next session of the government, and this document, P 05769 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. We sometimes continue thinking, and I'm also listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I hope you do Your Honour. So do I; I try anyways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, these are the minutes of the government meeting on the 9th of October, 1993. You'll see, in connection with the list of those present, among others, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Zubak, Mr. Stojic and, I believe, sir, Mr. S. Bozic. I take it, sir, that that's you, and this would be an occasion at least where both you and Mr. Stojic attended a government meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to ask you one thing, Mr. Scott, to make it easier for me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, the questions are asked by the Prosecutor, and you have to answer. This is the rule. Please, Mr. Scott, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You attended --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I don't mind answering any question, but I seem to feel that they want to trick me here in the courtroom, because first of all they're showing me a document from an HVO session, a collegium meeting, and then when I don't state my views, I'm moved to another document. So if that's the style of work, very well, I'll adapt to it. So that's why I reacted, not to avoid answering the questions. I know that the Prosecutor has every right, but I'm a little disconcerted -- I was disconcerted by the Prosecutor because he talked about General Matic, and then he went on to ask a question which he did not receive an answer to from me, and now he's moved me on to a completely different topic. So that's my reaction, but I will answer every question that Mr. Scott puts to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You can trust the Chamber, Mr. Bozic, and all the lawyers present that no tricks are played. There is a bunch of -- more than six high-quality lawyers. They're watching like eagles, and they will jump -- you have seen how easily they pop up, as it is said. So just answer the questions of Mr. Scott, and if there is a danger of some problem, you can be sure that it will be brought up by the lawyers, and the Chamber will also intervene. Please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, may I be allowed to say one thing. I'm a witness here who has taken the solemn declaration, and that is why I reacted; nothing more than that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Might I be allowed to say something, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, while you're on your feet, there is now a little problem between the Prosecution and the witness. Your name is mentioned in the minutes of this meeting. Just wait and see. We don't even know what the representative of the Prosecution wants to ask the witness. He's asked him, "Were you there on the 9th of October, 1993?" That's all we've heard. I don't know what he wants to say to the witness. Mr. Praljak, what did you want to say? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel said that somebody needs to stand up and say something if there is a misunderstanding, and I say that there is a trick in the sentence read out and ascribed to Mr. Lucic. May I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... talking about the lawyers, and this is the task of the lawyers and not of the accused. And you are not a lawyer, have you not even studied law, and I ask you to sit down and behave properly. I'm sorry, but we have to have some order here. And it is not a moment where you can take the floor, Mr. Praljak. I'm very sorry. Please, Mr. Scott. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'm not talking about the law. I'm talking about deception and trick. The lawyers failed to notice that trick. That is to my detriment, so I have the right to say where that deception is. You keep mentioning rights and the law. I can say that you don't know about electricity or the waterworks, or whatever. But let me say that there is indeed a great deception here presented by the Prosecutor in the sentence about Gabela and Dretelj which was uttered by Mr. Lucic. The easiest thing that the Judges can do is to ask the sentence be read out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague from the Bench was saying that there is no trick, when somebody asks a question to somebody. We're all looking for the truth. We're not trying to trick anyone. The Prosecutor has documents, and he develops his theory on the basis of these documents, and moreover to trick a former prosecutor or former judge is very difficult. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we're now on P 05769, and I believe that the only thing we've established so far -- the only question I put to you so far was that if this was a meeting that you attended, a government meeting you attended, and not only you, but apparently at least on this occasion, Mr. Stojic was also present. I believe your answer some minutes ago was, "Yes." Correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this meeting was attended by Mr. Stojic and myself and the other members of the senior staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on this particular occasion, in the minutes we can also see, can we not, the attendance of Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you will go to item 4 of this document, under "Conclusions," item 4: "The following is our position on the mobilisation of students. All students are conscripts, regardless of the location of study." Now, that was the resolution by the government of the very dispute between -- that we saw in the previous document, P 04756, involving Mr. Matic and the Main Staff, on the one hand, and Mr. Bagaric, Mr. Lucic, and Mr. Bozic on the other hand. Mr. Stojic said it would be presented to the next session of the government, and it's correct, is it not, sir, that we now see here Mr. Stojic did submit it to the government and the decision was made. The government sided with the position of the Main Staff that all students were conscripts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this subject was discussed at a meeting of the HZ-HB, but I must say that there was no conflict between the Main Staff and the Defence Department at the meeting of the 2nd of September that you're referring to. It was a discussion and a presentation of views by General Matic, as a military man, and the rest of us, who were civilians, and it wasn't a clash of interests. It was just a normal discussion and debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A normal discussion and debate where an issue was raised from the Main Staff to the Department of Defence to the HVO government; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Respecting the fact that students represented a separate category was quite logical that the University of Mostar had been set up, which had been dislocated or relocated, and that we held this discussion with representatives of the Education Department and the other members of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, you've also said that you did not see any documents concerning Mr. Stojic's involvement in military matters. But, sir, is it not the case that Mr. Stojic was regularly involved in military matters and that you were directly aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean in asking me that question. What are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked this question last week. I'm going to read it to you one more time. Page 36211 last week, I referred to it earlier: "Have you seen any document signed by Mr. Stojic which, by its content, would represent the commanding of armed forces or the use of armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I've never seen a single one." And I note, sir, that when that question was put to you by Defence counsel, you didn't have any problem understanding it, you didn't ask for any definitions, you didn't show any confusion. You answered the question directly [Realtime transcript read in error "You answered the question correctly"]: "I've never seen a single one." Now, that's what you said last week; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that last week, and I said the context in which I said those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P 01205.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which binder? Binder 1 or 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Binder 1, please. Just if I can correct the record when Mr. Bozic is talking -- excuse me, looking at the document. On page 33, line 10, it says the current -- the current transcript says you answered the question correctly. I don't think that's what I said, or if I did, I misspoke. But I think what -- you answered the question directly: "I've never seen a single one." Sir, if you have P 01205, this is a document by R. Pasalic from the Army of Bosnia Herzegovina in indicating the signing of a cease-fire agreement, indicating that Mr. Stojic would be signing that agreement, if you look at item number 2. You see that. And I'm going to show you another similar document before I ask you a question or two.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I do need the usher's assistance because another document has been opened up here before me. Thank you, I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please, next at P 02097, and also in the first binder, P 02097.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in this particular document, dated the 25th of April, 1993, we have a document -- an order signed apparently by both -- over the names, at least -- I don't want to get into signatures at the moment, but over the typed names of Bruno Stojic and Milivoj Petkovic, directing a cease-fire, ordering to all operative zones; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, Mr. Petkovic did not sign this document. He couldn't have signed it on that day, when the agreement in Zagreb was signed, but Mr. Akrap signed it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this order --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't ask if Mr. Petkovic signed it. This is an order issued over the signature -- over the names of Bruno Stojic and Milivoj Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the document was written as a result of the agreement, so it was signed in Zagreb on the 25th of April between Izetbegovic and Boban and Petkovic and Halilovic, the generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, do not documents P 01205 and P 02097 show that Mr. Stojic is, in fact, acting and being directly involved in military matters and the use of military -- in this particular, non-use of military forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. As far as I'm concerned, this is the implementation of an agreement which could not have been signed physically by General Petkovic, and in view of that fact, for that kind of decision to have the necessary authority to whom it is sent to, and that's all the operative zones, then the signatory was Mr. Bruno Stojic. If Mr. Petkovic had physically been able to sign this document, then I'm quite sure that this order would have been signed by him, himself, in keeping with the agreement that had been reached and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you just confirmed, sir, that Mr. Stojic did have military authority over all the operative zones and was therefore able to issue that order; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. What I said is that this order was signed on behalf of the Main Staff by Mr. Akrap, but due to the fact that everything -- that everybody wanted to stop the conflict, in keeping with the agreement signed by Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, it is my personal opinion, with which you do not have to agree, that for this to carry weight, and the fact that there would be no signature of General Petkovic, that Bruno Stojic's signature is on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P 07892, P 07892 in the second binder. This is the report by a special purposes unit known as the Vitezovi, dated the 18th of February, 1994. Sir, if you can find approximately the 10th item in the report. Unfortunately, the paragraphs are not numbered, but if you find that there is a paragraph that begins with the words -- and in English, Your Honours, it's towards the top of the second page: "On 24 October, after the outburst of hostilities between the HVO and the ABiH, Defence Minister Bruno Stojic ordered that the team return to the area of Central Bosnia." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's just look at the terms. On my copy, the date is the 18th of February, 1994. You mentioned some other date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I gave the name of the document, sir. In the document, on approximately the 10th paragraph of the document, you will find the words: "On 24 October 1992," which you might recall about the time of the events in Prozor, "after the outburst of hostilities between the HVO and the ABiH, Defence Minister Bruno Stojic ordered that the team, that is, the Vitezovi, return to the area of Central Bosnia." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Help me out. What page is that on? I don't see that. Give me the page number in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've indicated, sir, it's approximately the 10th paragraph in the document. If the usher can possibly assist you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May we zoom down on the English document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it, but it's not paragraph 10. Now, does it begin with the words: "After the conflict had broken out ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my translation starts with the words: "On 24 October 1992 ..." Now maybe it's the syntax of the B/C/S later in the sentence, but we appear to be looking at the same sentence. On the 24th of October, 1992, it mentions Bruno Stojic. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that: "On the 24th of October, after the outburst," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And later in the document, and I'll have to have the assistance of the usher because, again, there are no translations -- excuse me, there are no paragraph numbers, on the top of page --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll have to refer, Your Honours, to the ERN number stamped on the top of the page, and if I refer to the last four digits, I'm referring to 6511.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, several pages down in the text of the document you have, you will find this entry: "The report number 2-091/93 of 15 March 1993 was sent to the head of the Department of Defence, Mr. Bruno Stojic, and to the chief of the General Staff, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, that reported about the actions of the PPN Vitezovi during the conflicts in Central Bosnia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 15th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm referring to a report dated or for the 15th of March, 1993, going to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic. Correct? Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you go, please, to Exhibit -- Your Honour, I see the time. I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Work until a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You're absolutely right. My apologies. Jumping the gun, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have -- if you can next go to, if you haven't already, P 10807. And while you're doing that, I'll state for the record that this is an HVO document dated the 30th of January, 1993. The subject is: "Need for soldiers to be sent to Busovaca." And this purports to be an order by the vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, Colonel Dario Kordic. I'll ask you to look to the first paragraph of the document, above the word "Order." Mr. Kordic refers to this order being issued, quote, "with the approval of Bruno Stojic, chief of the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. With the best will in world, the usher can't help me out here, either. We can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Document P 10807. You see, sir, the first paragraph above the word "Order," where it talks about this order being issued with the approval of Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, "with agreement from Bruno Stojic," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, both documents P 07892 and P 10807, both show Mr. Stojic being directly involved in military matters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I apologise. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll read it back to you, sir: "Sir, both documents P 07892 and P 10807, both show Mr. Stojic being directly involved in military matters; correct?"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, I have my opinion, and I'll -- he was involved in a certain way, that would be my answer, which depended probably on the situation on the ground, what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look next at P 02292, P 02292 in binder number 1. While you're doing that, sir, if you can listen to me, I'll try and assist you by at least giving you some orientation to the document, and again as Judge Antonetti says, if I misstate something, I'm sure I'll be corrected. Sir, this appears to be a report by Zeljko Siljeg on the 11th of May 1993. It's addressed personally to Bruno Stojic, personally to Milivoj Petkovic, and it's Mr. Siljeg -- isn't it Mr. Siljeg giving a military report to both those gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, it is a report which is being sent to Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please, next at P 03124, again in the first binder, P 03124. Sir, this appears to be an order dated the 2nd of July, 1993, issued by Bruno Stojic to members of the civilian police, subordinating them to the military police, and ordering them into action or subordination again to the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd last like to remind you of the preamble above the order, where it says that it was -- that the military and civilians held this area together. So this was a joint effort by the civilian and military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I might try, Your Honours, to finish this topic with two additional documents before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, sir, to go next to P 03128 in the first binder, P 03128. Sir, this appears to be a -- again, a report by -- excuse me, my apologies. An order -- I flipped to the wrong document myself. This appears to be an order dated the 2nd of July, 1993, not only addressed to the head of the HZ-HB Defence Department, personally to Mr. Bruno Stojic, but if you'll look, sir, at the end of the document, is this not an order issued by Milivoj Petkovic, with Mr. Stojic signing and indicating his agreement with the order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but there's something illogical because here we have the head of the department and then he signs the agreement, which I suppose confirms that the seriousness of the situation required that kind of signing by Mr. Stojic of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why was the signature by Mr. Stojic required to indicate the seriousness of an order issued by the chief of the Main Staff? Didn't Mr. Petkovic speak with sufficient authority on his own, without requiring the additional signature of Mr. Stojic, or was it only Mr. Stojic who could issue this kind of order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't want to devalue the authority of General Petkovic, who was absolutely a person of high professional and human quality, but I said that the seriousness of the situation was such and that we should bear in mind that we're dealing with the 2nd of September, immediately after the treachery of a part of the HVO who were Muslims and the attack against the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar. So that's the reason why I gave the answer I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might be allowed, if we can look at Exhibit P 05232 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Mr. Scott. I'd just like to put right a mistake in the transcript. The witness, in line 22 of that page, or 20 of that page, said "the 2nd of July," and it says "the 2nd of September." So it should read "the 2nd of July."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, if you could please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- to P 05232, and we'll make this, if the Chamber allows, the last document before the break. Sir, this appears to be an order issued on the 20th of September, 1993, by Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. The transcript didn't catch the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. I think I had not activated the microphone. P 05232.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this order, sir, Mr. Stojic, and we don't have time to read the entire thing, but it basically says in item 1: "Engage all human and material resources in all free military and civilian police forces," et cetera. Number 2: "Muster these forces and place them under the command of the 1st Sector." And that's an order issued by Mr. Stojic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. But we must bear in mind that hunting organisations are mentioned here as well, which means anybody who had any weapons of any kind, that in keeping with this order they should respond and protect the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do not Exhibits P 02292, P 03124, P 03128 and P 05232 all confirm Mr. Stojic's direct involvement in military matters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have to agree with you, nor do you have to agree with me, so in my opinion that does not mean direct involvement. It depended on the situation, and perhaps in certain situations, because of the events on the ground, that it was that Mr. Stojic, in practice, appeared with his orders, but I, as a lawyer and as a layman in military terms, always consider orders to be for some concrete military operations and actions. If I'm wrong, then the Trial Chamber will weigh up my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding time, the Trial Chamber notes that the Defence had an initial 20 minutes. The Prosecution will then have five hours and twenty minutes, and so far you have used up two hours and forty minutes. You have two hours and forty minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to turn to the events in the Mostar area in early May of 1993. When I spoke with you in 2003, you had indicated that you did not have any knowledge that the Croats were ethnically cleansing the Muslims in Mostar in May 1993. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we were having lengthy discussions about ethnic cleansing, the theories behind it, and I even remember a statement of mine when I said that after the war, I read in an analysis done by an American organisation that the Croats were the greatest victims of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in proportion to the number of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not the answer to my question. Excuse me. I didn't ask you about what you read after the war. Is it your position, sir, before these Judges, that in May of 1993, you did not know that the HVO was conducting ethnic cleansing of the Muslims in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. The question, the way it is phrased, it's as if it is a fact. That is their theory, so it needs to be reformulated. I know -- you know, this is so evident. I mean, I hate to object, but this one, I have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that you did not know that members of HVO forces were moving Muslims out of their houses and moving them, for example, to the Heliodrom in early May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't know on what day this was, during my testimony in this courtroom, when I learnt for the first time that there was movement of civilians and -- from the combat areas and their relocation, and that this was part of the agreement between General Petkovic and Halilovic of the 12th of May, and I can't remember exactly whether it was the 17th or the 18th, at a meeting of the government, when there was a discussion about the department for those who had fled and what it had done in connection with the relocated civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to refer you and the courtroom to Exhibit P 10794, P 10794, which will be in the second binder. It's a copy of your -- in a previous interview. It's in five parts, and, Your Honours, if you don't recall from perhaps seeing it last week, each part is numbered separately, for better or worse. I'm now referring to the fifth part -- no, excuse me, the fourth part of the interview, part 4, page 48. In e-court, it's at page 214, if that might be easier for everyone in the courtroom, page 214 in e-court. If we can look at -- if we can look in e-court, in the interests of time, unless people have been able to find it, there's -- usher, there's not a B/C/S translation of that, so it won't really help, to be perfectly honest. Sir, I'm going to read to you very slowly and clearly, I hope, for the translation, so that I can put to you exactly the question and answers that I want to ask you about. For those in the courtroom who would like to follow and confirm that I'm reading the record accurately, slightly below the middle of page 48: "Q. Were you aware during May 1993 that the Croats were ethnically cleansing the Muslims from Mostar? Were you aware? Did you know it was happening? "Slobodan Bozic: I was not aware, since I did not have the information about it." Going across to page 49, the middle of the page, my question: "During this time, you didn't know -- you didn't see Muslims being expelled from their houses, being taken to the Heliodrom? You didn't see any of that going on or hear about it?" "Slobodan Bozic: I didn't see. I could only hear through the media, and I could also know later, since certain number of people were there, was there, and that later of people was later being released." Sir, can you confirm that your answer to my question on this topic, when we met before, was that you did not know about this, the moving of Muslims from their homes or to the Heliodrom at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. The answers that he gave are as they are on the paper. We can all see and read. The way now the question is being phrased is slightly differently. The gentleman indicated why he wasn't aware at the time. He didn't say that at no time he was aware of it. And also the first question, he was asked about ethnic cleansing, and then the question changed from ethnic cleansing to the people being transferred to the Heliodrom, which is a very big difference. So we can leave the record as it is, based on his statement, but I would object -- if the question is being posed, they need to be posed in a way that is fair to the gentleman so he can answer correctly. He did indicate last week where he was at the time when these events occurred and how he learned of those events. When you look at his statement -- his testimony last week and his statement in the -- that he gave to the OTP, they're identical in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we fully understood what you said, but as I told you earlier, we're not a jury from Arkansas, we're professional judges. We have the interview of the witness as a suspect. We have his answers, the question from the Prosecution, we have his answers today, we have the questions put today. The Judges will assess all this. Fine, you can intervene, you can take the floor, but let the professionals do their job. They understand what's going on. And to actually engage in law, I should tell the witness right now that he is entitled to say silent, that anything he says can be used against him, and so forth and so on. The witness is also a professional. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question pending to you at the time, and once again some lines of transcript go by, and we've lost the question on the page: Those were your answers to my questions. Sir, is it not true that at -- you said that at the time, not something you learned later, not something you read after the war, that at the time in May 1993, you did not know about the movement of Muslims in Mostar out of their homes and to the Heliodrom; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, in my statement -- I don't know whether it was on the first or second day, I said when I had learnt about those details or, rather, the situation when civilians were moved, and I stand by what I said on the first or second day of my testimony. I said that this was a topic that was mentioned for the first time at a meeting between General Petkovic and Halilovic and, secondly, that this was linked to certain activities, when talking about civilians under the Department for Expelled and Displaced Persons, and then I also saw it on the web page of Mr. Darinko Tadic. I appeal to the Chamber, since I am under oath, which makes me obliged to speak the truth, and I am speaking the truth, and I was in a situation when Mr. Scott questioned me for three days as a suspect. And after the first hour of my conversation, I could say to Mr. Scott, "My name is Mr. Slobodan Bozic, I was born on such and such a date, and I don't wish to answer any questions, I will keep quiet." That was my right which I didn't avail myself of. I wanted to be cooperative, and I still wish to be cooperative. And I've already answered this question, and I don't know why we're going back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... wasting my time, with all due respect to the Chamber. It is not my question, has nothing to do with the questions whether he was there, and what he felt at the time. He was represented by counsel, his rights were explained to him. We don't have to spend all the time. My question was very clear to him. I'll just move on, though, but I'm simply objecting to these long answers that are non-responsive, that are simply using the courtroom's time. Sir, you also said -- you did say at some point you learned this from the media. Which media did you learn from, and when was that? What media were you consulting at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, there were quite a number of media blockades throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, but there were some programmes - I don't know what their names were - picture on picture, or something like that, that was broadcast by Croatian Television, and I was able to hear and see what the media in Serbia were saying, the media in Sarajevo, the media in Macedonia, in Kosovo, in Slovenia, in Croatia, about one and the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned a meeting -- you tied some of your knowledge to the date of the meeting between Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic. Just so that we don't get that confused, can you tell us what date of that meeting you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a meeting I remember very well on the 12th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you participated in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was present at that meeting, and I spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
