utterances.text: Where was it, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, I think that meeting -- no, I'm quite sure that the meeting was held in the headquarters of the Spanish unit in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. You also mentioned reading something, and if the interpretation was correct, reading something on Darinko Tadic's web site. What web site was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, obviously it was a misinterpretation. I said that I was shown a document for the first time which was taken from Mr. Tadic's web page, when I was asked questions by Madam Nozica, and I commented on it, and you were in the courtroom when I said I was surprised by certain details from the contents of that document, and especially when he says publicly that due to his behaviour, that is, Mr. Tadic's, that he was congratulated by The Hague investigators. Allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I misheard you to say -- I misunderstood you to be referring to something you saw in May 1993 on the web site, and I do appreciate your clarifying that. That was the answer to my question. Sir, do you recall saying that during your interview, that in fact after leaving Mostar on about the 8th or 9th of -- excuse me, the 7th or 8th of May, a day or two before, that you did not return to Mostar until some five to ten days later?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I said in this courtroom, and that is that I left Mostar on the 8th, after a meeting attended by representatives of the European Troika, and that I didn't enter Mostar for a couple of days, but then I said that I was sure that I did enter on the 12th, in view of the fact that there was a meeting between General Petkovic and General Halilovic on that day, and then I went from Mostar to that meeting. And that is the correct answer, and that is what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your testimony, and when we were talking about where you were and what you were doing last week on the 9th and 10th of May -- excuse me. I'm referring to the daily transcript last Tuesday of what was then daily transcript pages 22 to -- 23 and 24, but it's a topic that I raised with you last Thursday, too, sir, if you may recall. You gave testimony last week about some things and what happened when you were having the telephone calls with the Spanish Battalion and the duty officer on the 9th of May, and I'll refer you to it again. You said because -- in response to Judge Trechsel -- excuse me for stumbling, but I'm trying to put this in exact context. In response to questions from Judge Trechsel about why you did not respond or call Mr. Stojic immediately, you said, and I'm quoting: "I did not see it fitting to inform Mr. Stojic, because in earlier situations, whenever problems arose, first I usually tried to delegate solving the problems to those who were affected by it, and if problems were of a major nature, then information would be relayed further up." Now, you referred to earlier situations whenever problems arose, you would try to delegate the solution of those problems. Can you give us an example, sir, of some of the earlier situations that arose by which you then delegated the solution of those problems?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier situations, if I were to think about them just now, it's a bit hard to remember, but I know that you asked me that, how I delegated the information that I received from European Observers in Mostar about the events in Ahmici, for example. That could be an example, in view of the fact that so much time has gone by, so I can't remember more examples. But I wish to explain what you just referred to, and I did so to His Honour Judge Trechsel, that earlier in the morning, he's not telling me that there's a conflict in Mostar; it was just a question of halting their transporter. And I tried to resolve it with someone who can deal with such a problem and who is in Mostar at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, on that occasion, let's take your specific situation. Who did you call or intervene with to solve the SpaBat problem on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it an intervention. I would call it information. I told Their Honours, and I think you can find this in the transcript, that I can't remember whether I called the duty officer in the Main Staff or the duty officer in the operative zone of South-Eastern Herzegovina in Mostar. In any event, it was one of these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you tell --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Spaniards had called me, that they had woken me up, that they had informed me that their transporters had been stopped at the entrance to Mostar, and in view of -- this is at least what I think, and Their Honours will decide whether my opinion is right or not. At all levels, military and civilian levels, the efforts were cooperative with respect to UNPROFOR and its movement, depending on the period --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... now taken it off into your opinion about movement. I asked you a very specific question. You said you intervened on that day with one or two people, either the duty officer of the Main Staff or someone in the operative zone. You've answered that question. My next question is: What did you tell them to do, specifically?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Scott. I didn't say that I intervened. I called up. That's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you tell them when you telephoned them? You had a conversation. What did you say, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please, but answer my specific question. Tell me what you said to the person you spoke to on the other end of the telephone.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called them up and I said -- let me try and paraphrase. And I said I have been called by the civilian section of the Spanish Battalion in Medjugorje, and they told me that their transporters had been stopped at the entrance to Mostar. I received an answer, that the Muslim forces had attacked the HVO, that the transporters had been halted for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... tell them what did you tell them to do. You had a conversation. At the end of that -- you've said -- you've said on earlier situations, whenever problems arose, "first I usually tried to delegate solving the problems to those who were affected by it, and if problems were of a major nature, that information would be relayed further up." You called this person, you spoke to them about this problem. Tell the Judges, what did you tell them to do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I am a witness of justice, and I'm repeating this for the umpteenth time in this courtroom. You might not like my answer. Whether it's truthful or correct, the Trial Chamber will decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask that you direct the witness to be responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd already put this question to you, and it seemed to be quite straightforward. The Prosecutor is just asking you what you said to the person on the other end of the line. It's very straightforward and simple, and your answer could be quite interesting, actually, it could be very interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, that is how I wish to answer, but obviously Mr. Scott doesn't like my answer, and that is why he's reacting in the way that he is. I said -- and allow me to provide my full answer, and then you will judge to what extent it is truthful or not. When I was woken up by the Spaniards, I called up the duty officer. I don't know whether it was in the Main Staff or in the command of the operative zone, and I told him that the Spaniards had passed on the information to me that their transporters had been stopped at the entrance to Mostar. The duty officer told me that the reason for this was the fact that the Muslim forces had attacked the HVO and that the transporters had been stopped for security reasons at the entry to Mostar. That is the answer which I think is identical to the one I gave to you a couple of days ago, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. Obviously, Mr. Scott wants me to say something else, and I don't wish to say anything other than what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you've just given the same answer that you've given us four to five times, without answering my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think your question is not quite correct, because it implies something. I think there are two questions hidden. First: "Did you give any indication that something should be done, that someone should do something?" The second question: "If so, what was it?" And maybe that could be helpful, if you divide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as a result of the telephone call, the person you got on the other end, and after you received all the information that you've told us about, did you give this person any directions or instructions as to what to do about the SpaBat vehicles which were stopped?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything to that person. I called the SpaBat from my apartment, and I told them that their transporters had been stopped for the reasons that I was given, for security reasons, because of the attack of the Muslim forces, and that it was only because of the security of their transporters and their staff, had they been stopped, until the matter was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's turn to some other events later that summer of 1993. Did you -- you've indicated before that you also didn't know about the arrest of Muslim men in the municipalities of Prozor, Capljina, and Stolac in July 1993. Do you recall telling me that, that you didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that when those arrests took place, I did not know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When do you recall first learning about them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I first learnt about them when there were exchanges and agreements about the exchanges of detained civilians as well as members of various armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as to Prozor and Stolac and Capljina, when was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I said when the exchanges took place. I can't remember, because it wasn't my work, it wasn't my job, so any answer I could give would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said that before, that concerning the situations in Mostar, the movement of the Muslims and then what I've just raised with you about the other arrests that were going on during the summer of 1993, you said you had no possibilities to do anything to prevent it. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any possibility to do anything because these were activities that had nothing to do with me and my duties. And I didn't know about many of those things, as I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's touch back on the HVO camps. You told me before that in fact you had never been to any of the HVO camps; is that correct? Did you tell me that, and is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I state, and I state it before the Honourable Trial Chamber, that I was never in any one of those prisons or camps or dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And also you still also maintain the position that you knew nothing about the conditions in those camps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew nothing about the conditions, except for what I learnt later on, as I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say you learned later on, when later on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said roughly that a lot of this information came when they were exchanged or, rather, when the prisoners were released from some of the prisons or dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You agree, do you not, sir, that the military prisons of the HVO were under the control of the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on what you mean by that question, when you say "under the control of the military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me see if I can assist you. Did you not give me this answer in your previous interview, and I'm referring for the courtroom to part 3 of the interview at page 40: "I know that military prisons were regulated or under the control of the military police"? That is what you said at the interview. Does that continue to be your position before these Judges today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "MR. IBRISIMOVIC:"] What I said then is what I say now, that it's a case of two military prisons and that the military police was the body which, in those military prisons, had their members who did certain duties and guarded the prison and had duties within the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the record is clear --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend, but there's a mistake in the transcript. The answer was ascribed to my colleague, Mr. Ibrisimovic. I'm sure that can be put right. It's says "Mr. Ibrisimovic," but I just wanted to step in on time to correct the transcript to avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, when you refer to the two military prisons, page 56, line 11, you're talking -- can we understand correctly you're talking about the Heliodrom and Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I meant and spoke about Heliodrom and Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we agree on at least this much, sir: That you have no dispute, you absolutely agree that the Heliodrom prison and Ljubuski detention facility were HVO military prisons which were under the control or regulation of the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the sense in which I understand "control" in those prisons, and the guards services and everything else, that in these prisons there were supposed to be military conscripts of the HVO, as well as other persons who committed certain acts linked to the regulations that were in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back to your previous testimony a few moments ago, where you said you'd never been to any of the camps and you were not aware of the conditions in the camps, at least not at the time. You must have known, sir, I put it to you, that there was immediate international media and international organisation outrage and coverage of these issues. You referred in several of your answers today to what you learned in the media. I put it to you, sir, as a senior Department of Defence official, deputy minister, had you no curiosity or felt no responsibility to go to those camps and find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I hear a question like that, Mr. Scott, then I have the feeling that you would like me to give an answer which suits you and which you would like. I was never in any prison, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... President's instructions not to continually make that statement to me. There's no basis for you to do so. I would appreciate if you could just go right to your answer. And I'm not judging whether I like your answer or not, sir. I'm taking your answers, and I'm also looking at the answers you gave in 2003, and I'm simply asking you questions. Now, whether I like it or not, sir, my questions -- and whether you like it and whether I like it, the question stands. Why didn't you go to any of these camps and try to learn what was going on? Paraphrasing, Mr. Karnavas, if necessary I will go back and read the transcript. I'm trying to assist the witness in moving forward. Sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer, or are you going to paraphrase what you mentioned about Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps there was a misinterpretation, sir. I put to you on line 57: "I put it to you, sir, as a senior Department of Defence official, deputy minister, had you no curiosity or felt no responsibility to go to those camps and find out what was going on?" Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that question. And as I've already answered many questions that you ask me at the time, that I'm a professional and that I've been doing my job, and that I occupied a high-ranking position at one time, and that I had subordinates, and in other cases I was subordinate. I did the jobs related to the position and place and role that I had, and let me just put you right. I wasn't the deputy minister, as you say. I was deputy of the head of the Defence Department for certain affairs, and in a situation like that, the kind that you mentioned, you could have told me why I had no interest in going to the front-line, for example, to see what was happening there and perhaps to stay in the trenches and fight with our combatants there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was very specific and had nothing to do with trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not answering the question, Witness. The Prosecutor wants to know why you didn't go to the prisons. Just tell us, I didn't go because it wasn't up to me; because I wasn't aware of what was going on; because I had no interest; somebody else should have done it instead of me. Please provide a very precise answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, perhaps I did answer, but gave a broad answer. It wasn't within the remits of my job, and I didn't have the possibility of knowing about that or of going to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I've heard a bit of two different things at different times, and I've heard you say -- on the one hand, I've heard you say that you didn't know. I've also heard you say that whatever you might have known, you couldn't do anything about. Can you clarify. Which is it, sir? Did you not know of the conditions in the camps? Did you not know that Muslims were being arrested and taken to Heliodrom? You did not know, or that you knew, but could not do anything about it, you felt?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not know, that I did not know, and that's my answer, that I did not know, and I repeat that for the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you did know, early in May 1993, that Muslim people were being held by the HVO, and you intervened at a number of situations specifically to have people released, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that your question is quite improper, especially in view of the questions you asked me earlier on, but I shall answer it nonetheless. I told you, in the conversation we had, that Mr. Boban happened to meet me in the hallway of the Defence Department and told me -- well, I can't say exactly whether that was on the 15th or 16th or 20th of May. At any rate, it was after the 9th of May. He said to me, and I can paraphrase what he said, he said, "Bobo," that's what they called me, Bobo, "you know a lot of people in Mostar. You have worked here, so we should resolve the situation as quickly as possible with these displaced persons who are located at the Heliodrom. And for the people that you know about or if anybody comes to you about certain people, then you should do what you can to resolve the issue and deal with the situation as soon as possible." So I apologise, Mr. Karnavas, but that has nothing to do with my knowledge about what was or what was not or what I did not do, and the period I knew about things or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll take the compliment of being compared to Mr. Karnavas, but I assume you're referring to Mr. Scott, to me, but that that's correct. Are you referring to me, sir, or are you referring to Mr. Karnavas, sitting across the room here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Yes, I looked at Mr. Karnavas. I apologise, Mr. Scott. I've become accustom to you. We have talked at greater length than Mr. Karnavas and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, be that as it may, let me just go back to this conversation with Mr. Boban, then. So you had this conversation with Mr. Boban sometime in the second half of May, perhaps as late as the 20th of May, and he said something to you about the Muslims being held at the Heliodrom, and if you can, do what you can to get some people released; is that basically the nature of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he roughly said that in view of the fact that I was in Mostar and knew a lot of people, that for the people that I knew of and whom I could help, and who I knew were down there, or if anybody were to contact me, that's important, to prevail on their behalf, that I should do what I could to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The conversation that you say you had with Mr. Boban, do you recall, in your interview statement -- let me start over again. Can you confirm today, as you said in your interview statement, that concerning this conversation with Mr. Boban, that Mr. Berislav Pusic was also part of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm the fact that Mr. Berislav Pusic was there, and I seem to remember a part of the statement that I made, and since you have your technology of examination, you asked me what I had said before. I said that maybe Mr. Pusic was there, but now I say that Mr. Pusic was not there, was not with Mr. Boban when he said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I didn't want to interrupt my learned friend Mr. Scott, but I think he overstepped the framework of the examination in chief. Nobody asked anything about Mr. Pusic in this courtroom, nor did Ms. Nozica in examination-in-chief, nor any of the other Defence counsel, so I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in the Court's hands, of course, as always, but I think it's relevant to the topic of the camps and the release of people, and this witness's involvement -- direct involvement with Mr. Pusic to get a number of people released. I believe it's directly relevant to the case, and he talks about his involvement with Mr. Pusic, or at least he did in his interview, extensively. But I leave it to the Chamber, whether the Chamber wants to hear about that or not. I believe it falls within the category of 90(H), of Rule 90(h).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the current conversation between you and the Prosecution focusses mostly on the use of terms. I think the Prosecutor speaks about detainees or arrested persons, whereas you speak of displaced persons, which is different. Now, when you talk about the people at the Heliodrom, you say that these persons were displaced, while Mr. Scott thinks they were detainees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps they were both displaced and detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's move forward and let's just see -- let's just see what develops in connection with how you tell us about some things. And, Your Honour, I don't think you can artificially separate from the narrative certain facts, but I'll leave it to see what the witness says. Sir, isn't it correct that following your at least -- I'll just say for the moment, at least following your conversation with Mr. Boban, you became involved in the release of various Muslims held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't put it that way, nor do I think that is the right observation, that I became involved in the release of various Muslims held by the HVO pursuant to an oral request from Mr. Boban. Now, knowing a certain number of people in Mostar, as I said earlier on, I tried to solve certain issues so that if I were to receive any information from someone's family or from some other party or side, then -- to the effect that the situation should be resolved as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how would you receive this information? You said you would receive information about people. How did you receive that information? And once you received the information, tell the Judges, please, very step by step, what did you do to get the people released?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but so far I have not intervened because I consider, and I know the Rules, of course, that the Prosecution can, on the basis of previous statements by this witness, possibly use them and differences in the statement to discredit the witness. However, I'm objecting now because the witness, during the examination-in-chief, was not asked with respect to these circumstances, and if the Prosecutor has other answers than received in the previous testimony, then the Prosecutor should put that to us and tell us what the witness said previously. The Prosecutor is now entering an area where the witness was not -- on which the witness was not questioned about. I'm just wondering whether that's the right road or not, and I leave it up to the Trial Chamber to reach a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will allow the Prosecutor to ask questions supportive of his own case. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I just want you to tell us, please -- you said you received information from time to time, and then I want you to tell where you received that information, how that would happen, and then what steps, if any, did you take to have people released from HVO custody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the way in which I received information was this: I received it from some of my friends and acquaintances, or from a family member of a person who had been displaced, and after that I would convey to Mr. Pusic what people were in question, because I know that there was a certain procedure which I didn't enter into. I would say who the people were and if there was no reason for detaining them further. And in view of the instructions given to me by Mr. Boban, well, Mr. Pusic would just receive information from me as to the names and surnames of the persons in question, the person who had been isolated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You called Mr. Pusic or contacted Mr. Pusic because you knew at the time that he was someone who was closely involved with the release of people being held by the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say that I knew that Mr. Pusic was someone who was closely involved in all that, but I knew that he worked in a team of people who dealt with those affairs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said in your previous interview that you would call Mr. Pusic to give him the names of people that you could vouch for, people that he had known before the war. How did you vouch for them? What assurances did you give Mr. Pusic on what basis these people should be released?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you at the time, and I'll repeat it here and now, that I guaranteed for these people because I knew them personally, but I always said, without knowing what might have happened in the meantime, that if there were no other obstacles coming from any other organs who were involved in checking these people out, then these would be my own personal impressions and my thoughts about these people and how I saw those people dating back to the time when I knew them, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... did you have to give? Guarantee as to what? Guarantee as to what? What were the criteria to have people released?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no guarantee or criteria, as such. There was just the instructions from Mr. Boban. And as I knew certain individuals personally, then I, as being me, Slobodan Bozic, not as deputy of the head of the Defence Department but as an individual, Mr. Slobodan Bozic, because he said, "Bobo, you see what you can do," so I personally guaranteed for these people because I knew them from the times before all these events took place. But I -- with the proviso that that would be the case unless there were other reasons to act otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You knew them. So what? Anyone that knows Slobodan Bozic should be released, and if you don't know Slobodan Bozic, you don't get released? So they knew you. So what? What were you guaranteeing? When you said you vouched for them, vouched for them in what way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I vouched for them as being people I knew, and now consciously or unconsciously, you are now trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you are repeating yourself, and obviously this answer is not what the Prosecutor is after. I do not know whether he's looking for something particular, but I think that his question goes towards a substance in the kind of, "I thought I was convinced, because I knew them, that these people would not take arms against the HVO, would not become political active against the HVO, would move to a certain place," something of that kind, you see. You speak that -- you say that you could vouch for them because you knew them. That is quite an acceptable answer. The question is: What danger could you vouch was not associated to releasing the persons? I don't know whether I translate the Prosecution correctly. Maybe this is completely wrong, and then Mr. Scott will correct me, but perhaps you could answer my question. What dangers did you think were not associated with the release of the persons concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I thought I'd already explained that, but let me explain again. First of all, I did this for people I knew, people I knew personally, Slobodan Bozic, and for whom I could vouch for. Now, I went on to say unless there were any -- unless there were other reasons or other impediments or facts which would make it impossible for them to be released. It didn't mean that my call to Mr. Berislav Pusic and the information I would give him about the people in question, it didn't mean that people -- these people would be released automatically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I cannot really find, in this, an answer to my question, but I -- Mr. Scott or -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance, Your Honour. Perhaps it is lost in translation, but the term "vouching," maybe you wish to ask what did he mean by "vouching." I think that might be a way to get to your answer, because I think that's what you're trying to get at, and perhaps something is being lost in translation. I'm only trying to be helpful with the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Bozic, can you explain what you mean by the term "vouching"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I knew someone to be a proper and correct person, for example, and if I was on friendly terms with them because they were such people, and I would even socialise with some of those people, so there were individuals also whom my friends said that they were friends of friends and that they were that kind of okay people, so that was the type of information. And I thank Defence Counsel Karnavas for helping me out about the word "vouch." It doesn't mean any document or anything like that kind, but my personal impressions, the impressions I gained as an individual about these other people. So if I could say that there were grounds for these people to be released, unless, as I said, there were no other reasons or impediments that could be raised by some other organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I were to translate your answer now into terms which are a bit not quite politically correct, perhaps, but if I sum up what you tell us, in a way it sounds as if you were telling us that you set free your cronies, people you -- people with whom you -- for whom you had sympathy, whom you wanted to assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I didn't release people who I liked, but this was to do with people whom I knew about through their families or whatever, through their families, family members, and I would propose them. So my proposal did not mean their ultimate release, and that's an important fact to remember. My proposal didn't automatically mean that those people would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I just -- and I want to inject another factor in here and then come back to some of these questions again. But when you were involved in these matters, did anyone from the HVO or on behalf of the HVO provide you with a list of detainees that you could then review and you could pick from the list those who you knew and those you could again, quote, "vouch for"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received such a list, and I never knew anything about such lists. I just said that I learned from my friends, acquaintances, or family members of the people who were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you contacted Mr. Pusic to get these people released, did you have to provide Mr. Pusic with any sort of documentation or was the mere fact that Slobodan Bozic vouched for these persons enough to get them released?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have to provide any documentation, no, we could speak on the phone. But I'm repeating for the umpteenth time that my call and my proposal did not automatically mean that they would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did it not occur to you at the time that if you personally knew people that should not be held, that there might be many, many others that you didn't happen to know of exactly the same situation? If you knew people that shouldn't be being held and you intervened to have them released, did it not occur to you at the time that there might be people not known to Slobodan Bozic that might be in the same situation and should be released?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had such an opportunity, perhaps I would try that too, but this was the possibility I had for the people I personally knew, and conditionally speaking, I provided the guarantees for those people. And you know what I told you at one point about the unpleasantness I went through because of such things and the stories that went around on account of my behaviour in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. My question to you is this: You held -- however you want to characterize it, I submit -- I submit to you and to the Chamber that you held a senior position in the HVO apparatus. I won't characterize it any further than that. The Chamber, the Judges, can draw their own conclusions. But I submit to you that you held a senior position in the HVO apparatus, and while you may have done something to intervene with a few people that you knew to have them released, what I want you to tell these Judges, as senior official of this apparatus, what official systematic steps did you take to see that people were released that shouldn't be held?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. It begs, first of all, some preconditions, whether he had the power to intervene and, if so, how he could intervene. The question presupposes that this gentleman had it within his right to go about and release anybody he wished. Now, I think he needs to lay some foundation, unless he just wants to put the question straight out and say, "I put to you that you had the power to release everyone from there, and you didn't do so," and then he can present the evidence to back his claim up. But he can't have it both ways, and I object to the form of the question. It's unfair. It's unfair to the witness, and I think we need to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree. I want the chance to respond before the Court rules. I disagree fully with Mr. Karnavas's position. The witness has spent the last half hour telling us that he could intervene on his personal -- on a personal basis without any documentation and on his vouching, get the release of people by calling Berislav Pusic, among other things. That's number 1. Number 2, I think after all these days of testimony so far, there is no dispute that Mr. Bozic, however else he may want to characterize it, held a senior position in the HVO apparatus. I submit to the Judges, Your Honours, that both of those items are enough foundation to put to the witness, "You knew that there were people that shouldn't be held because you've told us you intervened to have them released. We also know that you were a senior official in the HVO, and my question is: What did you do -- what steps, if any, did you take," did he take, to address the matter on not an anecdotal, "Well, I know a few people," but on a systematic basis as a senior official in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And my objection stands as it was. First of all, it presupposes that he had this ability. When he says he intervened, he was first asked by Boban, by his testimony. Secondly, he placed a call. Thirdly, he said repeatedly both to Judge Trechsel and to the Prosecutor's question that placing a call did not necessarily mean release. That's what he means by "intervention." And fourthly, he indicated that he would personally guarantee or vouch for the credibility of certain individuals whom he knew, not his cronies, and I thought it was a rather strong way of putting it, Judge Trechsel, but I take it that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I admitted, I admitted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know, you fessed up to it. But be that as it may, I think now we're over-reaching. Now, if Mr. Scott wants to lay some kind of foundation to show that he had the ability, but intervening by way of placing a phone call is a far cry from being able to actually open the floodgates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like the witness to answer the question. Witness, Mr. Scott put a question to you. Please answer. You do not need a counsel to know exactly what to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of this extensive debate, could Mr. Scott repeat the question so that I can make my answer clear and precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic, I put it to you that the evidence that you've given in the last half hour or so makes it abundantly clear, I submit - that's my submission to the Chamber and to you - makes it abundantly clear that you learned, at least at some point, and we'll put that -- we'll put the exact date to the side for the moment, but at some point you learned that Muslims were being held by the HVO, were in HVO-controlled facilities. You had the ability to call Mr. Pusic and at least ask to have people released, on your intervention alone, without documentation. I also put it to you, sir, that it is clear, I submit, clear to the Chamber that you held a senior position in the HVO apparatus, however else you want to characterize it. My question is: Based on the knowledge that you had, based on the fact that you were able to intervene to get people that you felt shouldn't be held released, what did you do on a more systematic basis? All well and good -- excuse me. All well and good for the individuals that you happened to know to get released, but as the deputy minister of defence, what were you doing to address the matter on a systematic basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I apologise for intervening. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you're about to say, Mr. Khan, but before you say anything, I must tell counsel that when a question is put either by you or by the Prosecutor to a witness, and that you or the Prosecutor stands up, this always -- there's always an impression that is given to the Judges. It feels like you want to lead the witness. That's the impression we get. But when the question is put and the answer comes spontaneously, then it gives a better weight to the answer. But now you have the floor. Go ahead. What do you want to say, Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Of course, appearances can be deceptive. Your Honour, it is relevant and of course it's a perfectly permissible question, but I cannot help but point out that at page 69, line 13 to 15, the witness was attempting to answer and explain issues that were -- it appears to me, at least, that were relevant to this line of questioning, and he was cut off by my learned friend Mr. Scott at line 16 of page 69. Your Honour, I think it is a problem, and it is an area that the witness is fully entitled to give an answer to, because it is of course germane to what he may or may not have done, and I would ask he be given the opportunity to answer what he was not allowed to answer previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott's question was very specific, Witness, so please answer the question put to you by Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll start with the last part of Mr. Scott's question. How highly placed I was and what I did, I've been talking about that in the past four days in this courtroom, and Your Honours will decide what my duties were and responsibilities. A second important thing which I wish to repeat is that I worked upon instructions from Mr. Boban in order to resolve the question of a certain number of people. Mr. Scott's question, whether I could have done the same for other persons that I didn't know, I could not because it was not within my remit. There were organs who were engaged in these areas and who decided about these things, and not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to turn, please, to Exhibit P 02380 in the first binder. Sir, this is a document dated the 14th of May, 1993, from Stanko Bozic, who the Chamber has heard evidence was the warden of the Heliodrom prison. Mr. Bozic here approves or confirms or communicates an order by Mr. Slobodan Bozic and Mr. Berke Pusic to release all persons -- excuse me, all ill persons to their homes immediately. Can you tell us, please, about you and Mr. Pusic issuing this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never issued this order. I remember this document very well, and we have had an extensive discussion about it when you investigated me as a suspect, and I told you that it was an example of an illogical order or decision, whichever you like. In the heading, we see the "Central Military Investigating Prison," the number and the date, and it says "Order." What order; oral, written, telephone, fax? And then he signs it himself. So as to avoid any error in the interpretation, I never communicated with Mr. Stanko Bozic by telephone, in writing, or orally. I told you then and I repeat now that this is an order that he gave himself. For what reason he mentions the name of Mr. Pusic and myself, only he knows, because I didn't have such competences, nor could I have given such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you knew Mr. Stanko Bozic before the war and had dealings with him prior to the 14th of May, 1993, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true, I didn't know him before the war. Obviously, you take something from the transcript that suits you and other things that don't. As far as I can remember, I said that I met him during the war as a person with the same surname as mine. We didn't know each other, and we live in different parts of town, and we engaged in different activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What were your relationship or dealings with Mr. Bozic prior to -- this Mr. Stanko Bozic, before the 14th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. We didn't even know each other personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so your suggestion is that Mr. Bozic -- Mr. Stanko Bozic simply just made this up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to say that he made it up. Whether by this order he wanted to show the justification of what he was doing, I don't know, but in any event he didn't receive any order from me, nor did I discuss this issue with Mr. Pusic ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you go, please, next to P 10 -- second binder, P 10792. Sir, this is a report by the ECMM, dated the 9th of June, 1993. I'd like you to look at, under -- well, first of all, under number 3, "Persons met," it indicates that there was a meeting with Deputy Minister of Defence HVO Slobodan Bozic, and then under number 5, in the second paragraph under 5, it says: "The visit to Mr. Bozic was a little tense. He asked about our work and why we wanted to visit the Heliodrom barracks. He was not pleased at all with this visit and tried to convince us not to go. We do not know of the reasons, but it could be related to the increase of fire in the city at that very time." Do you recall having a meeting around this -- did you have meetings around this time with the ECMM in May, June, July 1993? Excuse me, Your Honour, this is one of the documents that under certain procedures that -- we're allowed to use it in court, but it should not be broadcast. That's the only conditions, just that it should not be broadcast. Sir, can you tell us about your meetings with -- did you meet with the ECMM around -- during this time-period? You told us you were the liaison of international organisations. ECMM was one of those; correct? Sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part of this report am I asked to comment on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First answer my question. Can you confirm to us, sir, that during May, June, July 1993, that you had regular meetings with ECMM?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mean unofficially I did meet with them. I can't say regularly. It depended on the case, and I did meet with ECMM monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean you did mean unofficially? That's at least how it came out in the transcript. Were you meeting with them in your official capacity or unofficially?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an error, not "unofficially." I said from one case to the next and not regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, around the 9th of June, 1993, being asked by the ECMM that they wanted to visit the Heliodrom barracks and you trying to convince them not to go to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in this report, the problem may be related to the surname. Under item 3, they say they had a meeting with me, and then in item 5 they speak of the impossibility to go to the Heliodrom, access to the Heliodrom, and there is reference to Bozic who was in charge of the prison and not the Bozic that they met and which is referred to in item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the only Bozic they refer to in this record of meetings for that day, item 3, "meetings/people met," and the only Bozic that they referred to as having met in connection with this report is a meeting with the deputy minister of defence of HVO, Slobodan Bozic, and that's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you're not right. Under item 3, they talk of a meeting that they had with me, and in item 5, we can read it verbatim for the Trial Chamber to see: "Visit to the hospital will result in an official request by UNPROFOR to change the medical personnel, seven doctors, with specialists of the West Bank. Team had no access to the Heliodrom barracks at 16.30 hours." In continuation: "Visit to Mr. Bozic was a little tense. He asked about our work and why we wanted to visit the Heliodrom barracks. He was not pleased at all with this visit," et cetera. They're talking about them being prevented by Bozic to visit the Heliodrom and not to the Bozic that they spoke to and which is referred to in item 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please forgive me, but upon instructions from His Honour Judge Antonetti, I waited for the answer so that my intervention could not assist the witness, but the report says that the meeting with Mr. Slobodan Bozic was held at 9 hours. This is what it says at item 3. And could my learned friend look at the whole document. And this second visit certainly took place after 16.30 hours, because that is when UNPROFOR was prohibited from entering. So obviously these were two different meetings, at least judging by the time when they were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree with that characterization, but now counsel are simply arguing the evidence, and I'll move on to the next document. If you could turn next, sir, to Exhibit P 02260 in the first binder, P 02260.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this appears to be a report dated -- or official note, it's called, just to be very specific. On the 10th of May, 1993, referring to the arrest and the holding of -- let me just -- at the risk of being accused -- so I will not be accused of paraphrasing, it says: "A decision was issued that all ethnic Muslim citizens from the right bank of the Neretva were to be quarantined in the SVZ in the Heliodrom." Can you tell us, sir, who on behalf of the HVO made that decision, a decision, "a decision was issued that all Muslim citizens," et cetera. Who at the HVO made that decision?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who made such decision, and this is the first time I'm seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who would have the authority in the Mostar region to issue such a decision, based on your familiarity with the Department of Defence and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is nothing to do with the Defence Department. There is mention of people who were not in the HVO or the Defence Department, a gentleman and a lady, so whatever I would say would be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how soon after this decision did you become involved in getting people released?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't comment on what you are saying involved. It's a rather harsh qualification. I would prefer to say that upon instructions from Mr. Boban, I tried to solve the problem with a certain number of people, for them to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it may be about time for a break, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two questions on semantics, Mr. Witness. I'm a legal expert, I listen to the Prosecutor, I listen to what you're saying, and I'm also looking at the document. On this document, I note the following "May 10th," which is the day right after May 9. This document comes from the Central Military Prison. It says that there was an attack by the MOS on the 9th of May, and that after that someone - we don't know whom - decided that these Muslims were going to be quarantined. I would like to know what is the word in your own language for "quarantine." I'm trying to look at the B/C/S text, and I can't find the word for "quarantine." Is it "izoludju [phoen]"; would that be it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, this word, "izoludju," what does it mean in your language and in your legal system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we were to define it, I'm not really a linguist, but it means removal of a certain number of persons who would be protected and under the control of certain organs or bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the former Yugoslavia, could you tell us whether there was a legal text that would make it possible to isolate a number of people, quarantine them or place them in custody, administrative custody or something? Was there a legal text that would allow for this and provide for this? Let me give you an example. Imagine an illegal alien, a foreigner who would be in the Republic of -- in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and had nothing to do there. What could the authorities do? Would they put him in custody? Would they put him in jail? Would they take him to an investigating judge? How was the problem of illegal aliens solved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't like to speculate, but I think that there was the possibility for isolation in certain centres, conditionally speaking centres, since we're using the word "isolation," in the centres for isolation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English text, we have the word "release" at one point in time. Now, in B/C/S, could you tell us what is the word for this situation, what is the word used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could you tell me which part of the text you're referring to when you're using the word "release"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the paragraph before last in English, but you don't know English, but it says that these people can be released, and we have the word "release" twice in the text, because Mr. Pusic can also release these persons. So what is the word used in your own language, in this document, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document, the word "liberate" is not being used, because as lawyers, it would mean that somebody is serving a sentence. So in this case, they're referring to "otpustanje." If somebody was isolated for security reasons, then he is released. So it doesn't mean "liberation." We lawyers would use "release" if there was a judgement of acquittal. Here the word used is "otpustanje" in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So they're released, let go, whereas in English it's "release," but in English you can only be released if you've been detained, whether if you're let go, it's a bit different. I just wanted this to be noted down, and I believe that everybody should reflect on this now. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated previously, when we spoke before, that it was possible that you had helped a man named Zoran Mandelbaum get certain people released from the Heliodrom. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and you showed me that we had a talk -- or when we had a talk, when I was in the capacity of a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandelbaum was a witness in the Tuta, Stela case. Actually, I believe, he was a defence witness, but I showed you or I put to you some of the testimony from that case where he indicated -- he swore in that case that you had helped him to get some people out of the Heliodrom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not to pull some people out of the Heliodrom, but in the same way that I spoke earlier on, in conformity with the instructions from Mr. Boban, I helped Mr. Zoran Mandelbaum as well, whom I knew far before these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You testified earlier today, sir, that you had never been in any of the HVO camps and you didn't know the conditions there. But Mr. Mandelbaum says that in his connections with you, getting people released from the Heliodrom, he rode with you in a jeep to the Heliodrom for the purpose of getting people released. Now, do you recall, does that refresh your memory about actually going with Mr. Mandelbaum to the Heliodrom to obtain the release of certain people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true, nor did I ever go with Mr. Mandelbaum to Heliodrom, nor was I ever at Heliodrom, nor did you ever tell me that when you interviewed me with a suspect. You just told me part of Mr. Mandelbaum's statement to the effect that I had helped him -- well, conditionally speaking, I said how that happened, in what way, for certain individuals to leave Heliodrom, but you didn't tell me that then. And what you're saying now is not true, and it is incorrect that I ever got into a car with Mr. Mandelbaum, let alone go to Heliodrom with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum testified that first you had gone to Berko Pusic and you didn't get any satisfaction from Mr. Pusic and, quote: "I went to Mr. Slobodan Bozic, who got his jeep ready and brought two of his colleagues along." And then he goes on to talk about how you went to the Heliodrom. So you're saying that Mr. Mandelbaum is wrong in that regard? You reject any possibility that you went with Mr. Mandelbaum to the Heliodrom to have people released?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely exclude that possibility. And let me repeat, when you interviewed me as a suspect, you just put to me part of the statement, saying that I had helped Mr. Mandelbaum. Now everything you're saying now has nothing to do with what you asked me then at the time when, let me repeat, I was interviewed as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've said that all day long. Are you telling the Chamber that you gave certain answers when you were interviewed as a suspect, and you give different answers when you come to court? What are you trying to tell these Judges? So you were interviewed as a suspect. So what? Are you saying you gave different answers then than you're giving now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're wrong on that score. I did not give different answers. I gave the same answers then and now. But you didn't ask me at the time, nor did you make any mention of any vehicle, any jeep, or my going to Heliodrom, or anything of that kind, so that's the difference that I'm referring to. But otherwise, I'm saying the same thing now as I said then, as a suspect, and I confirm that to the very last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your -- about these people that you got released, you have said before in your interview -- if we need to turn to, we can. But if we can save some time, it will be appreciated, but certainly if you want to look at it, we can. You said, in relation to the people that you obtained their release, "certainly these people are alive today, they are healthy and alive, because of your intervention." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I'm happy if they are alive and well, those people who left that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that takes us back to this topic that we discussed before. And so it sounds -- I put it to you, it sounds to me that the people who were -- maybe in this regard, who were fortunate enough to be alive today, are alive and healthy in connection with you, simply because they happen to know Slobodan Bozic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people left because Mr. Boban gave me those instructions, and then I tried, when at all possible, when I knew about certain things and was in -- or, rather, certain people and was in a position to do so, I tried to see that the question was resolved. But the essential point in this courtroom, it seems, is to repeat the same thing five times, so I have to repeat it again and say that I provided information and data about those individuals, but that did not automatically mean that they would be released, if there were any other reasons for detaining them further. So I didn't make the decisions. I just initiated the process of their release.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said previously that you weren't sure how many people were actually released. You said just now you don't know if they were released or not. But you do know, didn't you, and you said, talked about some, that you actually obtained their release or their letting go, to follow up on the conversation before the break. You know that, sir, don't you? You're not telling this Chamber that you don't know. You know that certain people that you intervened on their behalf, that they were released, and they were released because they knew Slobodan Bozic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were released because I initiated their release because I knew who the people were, what kind of people they were, and I respected the instructions given to me by Mr. Boban. And the fact that this -- the fact that I initiated the process didn't actually mean that they would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you keep talking about this conversation with Mr. Boban, but you've told us, and you've confirmed this much, and that is: During this time-period, May and June 1993, you were sitting in the Ministry of Defence offices, you shared a secretary with Mr. Stojic. Mr. Stojic was across -- adjacent to your office. You were in shouting distance of Mr. Petkovic. Now, are you telling these Judges that throughout this time-period, there was no discussion with Mr. Stojic, no discussion in the hallway, no discussion going downstairs to Mr. Petkovic's office about the holding of Muslims by the HVO and what the HVO was going to do about it on a systematic basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't talk to Mr. Petkovic or, rather, General Petkovic or Mr. Stojic, and the period of time that you're referring to was the time when we were dislocated or, rather, moving, so we couldn't see each other on a daily basis. But regardless of that, neither with General Petkovic, nor with General Stojic, did I discuss that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, really, the same question, sir: Why not? This is a huge issue. It's on CNN, it's on BBC. There's film footage. The Judges have seen footage of men and women being led from Mostar to the Heliodrom. It's a huge world issue, and you didn't talk about it with the person across the office from you, Mr. Stojic, or Mr. Petkovic, who was working in the same building? And if you didn't, sir, why not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered that question earlier on. I said that I had no need to discuss it with them because that wasn't part of my job. That's the first point. And, secondly, I know that there were organs or, rather, services which dealt with that kind of thing, so in my personal opinion, anything else would be my meddling. And as a professional, I never wished to meddle in other people's affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Some people might call "meddling" managing, as a deputy minister; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said -- I said that throughout my life and my career, I operated in such a way as not to meddle into the affairs of others. And today, too, I have my job, and I do part of my job independently of what my colleagues do at the head of other sectors within the company that I run.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you please look at P 10782 in binder number 2. P 10782. 10782. For some reason, it doesn't seem to be in the binder. Can we have the assistance of e-court, please, or if it's loose. It doesn't seem to be in the binder for some reason. If we can work in e-court, it would be most appreciative, just to save time. Sir, this is a document dated the 22nd of July, 1993, over the name of someone named --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to start up the discussion of last week, but I'd like to object again and say that this document is being introduced into the proceedings contrary to the Trial Chamber's ruling of the 27th of November, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, although we're not dealing with General Petkovic's interests in this document, I would like fully to support Mr. Ibrisimovic's objection, and I consider that with respect to these documents, we ought to behave pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision that we discussed last week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, this document was not a 65 ter document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was on the 65 ter list, Your Honour. I think it's true to say that it was not admitted during the Prosecution case, but I'll ask Ms. Winner to confirm that. But again I must say, and this came up last week, I'm not aware of any rule which requires cross-examination material to be listed on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has decided that you could use this document to test the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have found -- if you can go on e-court, and I apologise, to the last page of the document, please. I can't give you the number, but it's the last page, unless Ms. Winner can assist me -- there you go. And if we can have it in English as well, please. Thanks very much. Sir, this is a document, as I was saying, dated the 22nd of July, 1993, over the typed name of someone named Ivan Bandic, and I'd just like you to look at the last item, which in the English is marked as 221, and then it appears to be 216 for whatever reason. I think it's just a typo. It's on the list -- English list, it's 213, 214, 2 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask a question? May I be allowed to ask a question, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait. Wait until we hear the Prosecution's question, and if there is a major problem, then you'll be allowed to intervene.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say something, since this is a friend of mine who's not alive, so may his name be left out, not mentioned, and I'll be happy to comment on anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the person that's listed in the last of this list, number 216? Next to that name is your name, Slobodan Bozic. Do you recall helping that individual obtain freedom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, and that's why I asked the Trial Chamber what I asked a moment ago. It's my friend who's no longer alive, and I used the same procedure, pursuant to Mr. Boban's instructions, and applied it to this particular person as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, just a couple of questions, perhaps, on the topic of forced labour. You recall telling me, during your interview in 2003, that again you did not know -- you had no knowledge that the HVO was using prisoners in forced labour; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said at the time that I did not know that the HVO used prisoners for forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you ever at some point learn the contrary, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all that was later, a lot later, much after those events and the situation that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So just so the testimony is clear, throughout this time, that is, from -- let's talk about, as we have been primarily, May and the summer of 1993, into the fall of 1993, your testimony to the Judges is throughout that time-period you did not know that the HVO was using prisoners in forced labour. That's your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. As far as I remember, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you would agree, sir, and you confirmed to me when we spoke before, that to use prisoners in forced labour would be improper?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any forced labour is unlawful, and any coercion is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned earlier today that when you learned about the events that had happened in Ahmici in mid-April 1993, that you reported that to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I said quite precisely, after I was informed by an officer, an observer from the European Union, I think it's the name you mentioned frequently, I think it was Mr. Christopher Beese, that after that -- it was after that that I informed Mr. Stojic and General Petkovic, and that that was as far as I remember, and when I look at some documents that I had seen, it was after the signing of the agreement between General Petkovic and General Halilovic, which was on the 25th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you did say, sir, that you immediately reported the news to Stojic and Petkovic. In one place, you said: "At the very same moment I finished with him," referring to the EU Monitor, "I reported to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic about it." So you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I learnt about it and received the information from the EU Monitor, I informed General Petkovic and Mr. Stojic about that. And when I added the date, since I have seen a large number of documents, I just added that all this happened after the 25th of April. So I'm not changing my testimony. I just added the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you reported this to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic, did either of them give you any indication that this is something that they already knew about, or did you have the impression that you were telling them something for the first time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want my frank and sincere answer, and I have to give you a frank and sincere answer because I'm under oath, at the meeting, and this is very important in view of your question, at the meeting that was on the 19th of April in Medjugorje, which came before the meeting of the 25th in Zagreb and the signing of the agreement, nobody, I repeat nobody, by a single word mentioned Ahmici, and the meeting in Medjugorje was on the 19th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you didn't exactly answer my question. When you reported Ahmici, the information about Ahmici to Mr. Stojic -- let's take them one at a time to make it as simple as possible. Let's take Mr. Stojic first. Was Mr. Stojic surprised? Did he react to you as something he had not heard before? Or did you have the impression that he already knew about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that when you interviewed me as a suspect, that it was a surprise to Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic, because I think that on that day, whether by APCs or helicopter, somebody or, rather, General Petkovic or someone else started out towards Central Bosnia, so that statement, although I have gone it here in front of me - you have it in the English version - that's what I said then when I was answering your questions as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know how Mr. Petkovic travelled to Central Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said whether it was a helicopter or APCs, I'm not quite sure, because it was at the time when negotiations were underway about the formation of a joint staff, a joint command, which in actual fact was a continuation of the Medjugorje agreement of the 19th of April or, rather, the Zagreb agreement on the 25th of April, 1993. I can't be sure whether it was a helicopter or what, or APCs, and whether they were supplied by the EU or whatever. It would be guess-work on my part if I were to opt for either one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on receiving the information about Ahmici, why did you report it to Stojic and Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a logical step to take, in view of the position that I held. I worked with affairs on behalf of the Commission for Cooperation with UNPROFOR, covering part of the affairs relating to the defence area. Now, I think it was Mr. Beese who told me, who said that what happened had happened, and that he had said that certain armed persons, soldiers of the HVO, had committed what they had committed. Then it was logical for me to inform Mr. Stojic about that, as well as Mr. Petkovic or, rather, General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any further involvement after that time with any investigations or inquiries by the HVO into the events at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't involved further in any investigations or inquiries. And as I said, that wasn't within my remit, the remit of the post and job I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you don't know, is it correct, when you told me before, and would you confirm again today, that you don't know and never knew at the time whether any HVO soldiers were ever punished or disciplined for the events at Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said then, I can repeat and confirm now. I said that I did not know whether anybody was punished, or disciplined, or held responsible, and I said, if I remember correctly, that it wasn't a question of disciplined -- of being disciplined, but I think I remember that what I said then is what I say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us throughout your testimony that you were a principal liaison with the international organisations. Ahmici was certainly an ongoing topic of some controversy and notoriety. Did you have no continuing interest or curiosity concerning that event, or what happened, or if anyone was punished, or if anyone was disciplined, or if anyone in the HVO, anyone in the Department of Defence, of which you were deputy minister? Was -- anything happened -- was there consequences of that event?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN BOZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that it wasn't within my remit.
